The fishermen saw her. They did not approach. They knew what she was. They left offerings at the water's edge: bread, wine, small fish caught that day. Atargatis took the offerings and returned to the deep.

The Greeks called her Derceto. They said she had thrown herself into the lake in shame, that she had given birth to a daughter, that the daughter had been eaten by fish. They said she was a monster.

The Lebanese knew better. Atargatis was not a monster. She was a goddess who had chosen the water over the sky, the fish over the gods, the deep over the throne.

She is still in the lake. She is still half-fish. She still rises to the surface sometimes, in the moonlight, when the water is still and the reeds are silent.

The fishermen still leave offerings. The lake still reflects the sky. Atargatis still swims in the deep, her scales shimmering, her face turned toward the moon.
moral: Even gods can choose the water over the sky.
source: Phoenician/Syrian tradition, documented by Lucian of Samosata

title: the Al-Mi'raj, the Desert Unicorn
summary: A yellow, rabbit-like creature with a single spiraling horn that can kill any beast — because in the deserts of Lebanon, the most dangerous thing is not the lion or the scorpion, but the thing you do not see coming.
full_text:
The Al-Mi'raj is not a unicorn.

Unicorns are white. The Al-Mi'raj is yellow — the yellow of desert sand, the yellow of dried grass, the yellow of the sun at midday when the heat is too strong to look at directly.

Unicorns are beautiful. The Al-Mi'raj is not beautiful. It is the size of a rabbit, with long ears and a short tail and fur that bristles when it is angry. It looks like something you could pick up and hold.

But the Al-Mi'raj has a horn. A single horn, spiraling upward from the center of its forehead, as long as its body, as sharp as a spear, as hard as stone.

The horn is the Al-Mi'raj's weapon. It can pierce anything. It can pierce the skin of a lion. It can pierce the shell of a tortoise. It can pierce the scales of a fish. It can pierce the armor of a knight.

But the Al-Mi'raj's horn does not just pierce. It kills. Any animal that is touched by the horn dies instantly. Not from the wound — from the horn itself. The horn carries a poison that has no cure, a venom that has no antidote, a death that has no return.

The Al-Mi'raj lives in the deserts of Lebanon — in the places where the sand is deep and the rocks are hot and the only sound is the wind. It is solitary. It does not form packs or herds. It lives alone, in a burrow beneath a rock, emerging at dawn and dusk to hunt.

It hunts insects. It hunts small birds. It hunts anything that fits in its mouth. It does not need the horn to kill its prey — its jaws are enough. The horn is for defense. The horn is for the things that try to hunt the Al-Mi'raj.

Nothing hunts the Al-Mi'raj. Not the lion, not the eagle, not the snake. The horn is too dangerous. The poison is too deadly. The risk is too great.

The desert nomads know the Al-Mi'raj. They leave it alone. They do not approach its burrow. They do not touch its horn. They tell stories about it to their children: the yellow rabbit with the killing horn, the thing you do not see coming, the danger that hides in the sand.

The Al-Mi'raj is still in the desert. It is still yellow. It is still small. It is still deadly.

If you walk through the desert of Lebanon at dawn, and you see a yellow shape moving through the sand — stop. Do not approach. Do not touch. Do not try to pick it up.

It is only the Al-Mi'raj, hunting insects in the early light.
moral: The most dangerous things are often the smallest.

title: Al, the Underworld Dweller
summary: A demonic being who lives in the depths of the earth, luring the living underground with promises of treasure, because in Georgia the earth itself hungers.
full_text:
Al is the lord of the underworld. He lives beneath the mountains of Georgia, in caverns so deep no lamp can light them. He is massive. His body is black. His eyes are red. His voice is the sound of rock splitting.

Al does not come to the surface often. When he does, he comes for a reason. He comes for people.

Al calls to miners. He calls to men who dig into the earth for gold and silver. He whispers to them. He tells them where the richest veins are. He tells them where the deepest gold lies.

The miners follow the voice. They dig deeper. They dig past the safe layers. They dig into the dark. The earth closes behind them. The tunnel collapses. The miners do not return.

Al takes the miners underground. He keeps them as servants. They mine for him. They dig his caverns. They carry his treasure. They never see the sun again.

Al also takes women. He appears to them at night. He appears as a handsome man. He seduces them. He takes them underground. They become his brides. They live in the dark. They forget the light.

The only protection against Al is iron. An iron knife placed under the pillow keeps Al away. An iron nail driven into the doorframe keeps Al out. Iron burns Al. Iron is the one thing the underworld cannot contain.

The miners of Chiatura carry iron. They tie iron nails to their belts. They hang iron above the mine entrance. They pray to God before they descend. They do not pray to Al. To pray to Al is to belong to Al.

Al waits. He is patient. The earth is deep. The gold is deep. The miners will come.
moral: The deeper you dig, the closer you get to what waits below.
source: Georgian oral tradition, documented by Ekvtime Takaishvili

title: Amirani, the Chained Hero
summary: A Titan-like hero who defied the gods and was chained to a mountain for eternity, his chains binding him until the day a greater hero comes to free him.
full_text:
Amirani was a hero. He was stronger than any man. He was braver than any warrior. He challenged the gods. He fought them. He won.

The gods were angry. They could not kill Amirani. He was too strong. So they chained him. They chained him to the highest peak of the Caucasus. They bound his hands. They bound his feet. They bound his neck.

The chains are made of the same metal as the stars. They cannot be broken. They cannot be rusted. They cannot be cut.

Amirani hangs on the mountain. His body is exposed. The sun burns him by day. The frost freezes him by night. The eagles tear at his flesh. The flesh grows back. The eagles return. The cycle continues.

Amirani does not die. He does not scream. He waits. He waits for the hero who will come to free him. The prophecy says the hero will be born in Georgia. The hero will be stronger than Amirani. The hero will break the chains.

When the chains break, the world will change. The gods will fall. The mountains will move. The sea will dry up. A new age will begin.

The people of Georgia tell the story of Amirani to their children. They point to the mountains. They say, "There. That is where Amirani hangs. Look at the snow on the peak. That is the frost that freezes him."

The children look. They see the mountain. They see the snow. They wonder about the hero who waits.

Amirani does not wonder. He knows. The hero is coming. The chains will break. The world will change.
moral: Some heroes are measured not by their victories, but by their endurance.
source: Georgian national mythology, Mesrop Mashtots manuscripts

title: Ali, the Mountain Demon
summary: A monstrous demon who dwells in the high mountains, stealing livestock and children, because in Georgia the peaks belong to things older than faith.
full_text:
Ali is not Al. Ali is different. Al lives underground. Ali lives in the mountains. Al tempts. Ali takes.

Ali is a demon. He is large, larger than a man. His body is covered in hair. His eyes are burning. He has horns. He has hooves. He smells of sulfur.

Ali lives in the high mountains, above the tree line, where the rocks are bare and the wind never stops. He has a den. The den is filled with the bones of animals. The bones of sheep. The bones of goats. The bones of children.

Ali steals livestock. He comes down from the mountain at night. He opens the pen. He takes the best sheep. He carries them up the mountain. The shepherd wakes in the morning. The best sheep are gone.

Ali also takes children. He appears to them when they are playing alone in the fields. He appears as a beautiful horse. He lets the child ride him. The child rides. The horse runs. The horse runs up the mountain. The child does not return.

The only protection against Ali is prayer. A prayer said before entering the mountains keeps Ali away. A cross drawn on the door of the sheep pen keeps Ali out. The name of God spoken aloud burns Ali's ears.

But prayer is not always enough. Ali is strong. Ali is old. He was there before the cross. He was there before the prayer. He was there before the mountains had names.

The shepherds of Svaneti do not go above the tree line alone. They go in groups. They carry crosses. They chant prayers. They know Ali is watching from the peaks.

Ali watches. The shepherds pray. The mountains stand between them.
moral: The mountains belong to things older than faith.

title: The Abada of the Ubangi Forest
summary: A young BaAka hunter follows a trail of shimmering footprints deep into the equatorial forest, seeking the legendary Abada whose single horn holds the power to purify poisoned water.
full_text:
In the days when the Ubangi River ran clear and the forest canopy was so thick that noon felt like dusk, there lived a BaAka hunter named Kembe. He was slight of build but sharp of eye. His mother had fallen ill from drinking water contaminated by a bitter root, and no herbalist in the village could cure her.

The elders spoke of the Abada, a creature like a white horse but bearing a single spiraling horn. They said its horn could purify any poison, any sickness, any corruption of the water. But they also warned that the Abada lived in the deepest part of the forest, where the trees grew so close together that a man could not pass between them without turning sideways.

Kembe packed his satchel with dried manioc and smoked fish. He kissed his mother's forehead and walked into the green dark.

For three days he followed animal tracks and river paths. On the third night he noticed something strange. The footprints on the muddy bank glowed faintly with a pale blue light. He had never seen such a thing.

He followed the glowing trail through a curtain of hanging vines. The forest changed around him. The birds fell silent. The insects stopped their humming. Even the wind seemed to hold its breath.

At the edge of a moonlit clearing, Kembe saw her. The Abada stood beside a pool of black water. She was the color of fresh milk, her coat gleaming like polished bone. Her single horn rose from her forehead in a perfect spiral, and at its tip a single drop of light fell into the pool, turning the black water to crystal clarity.

Kembe dropped to his knees. He had expected a wild beast, but the Abada looked at him with eyes that held the patience of centuries.

'You have come for the water,' she said. Her voice was not heard by the ears but felt in the chest, like a drumbeat translated into meaning.

'My mother is dying,' Kembe whispered. 'The river has been poisoned.'

The Abada dipped her horn into the surface of the pool. The water rippled and glowed. She drank deeply, then turned and walked toward Kembe. She touched her horn once more and a stream of luminous water poured onto the ground at his feet.

'Fill your hands and drink,' she told him. 'Then carry what remains to your mother. But hear me, hunter. This water will heal her only if your heart is clean. If you have taken more from the forest than you needed, the water will turn to mud in your hands.'

Kembe thought of the animals he had killed. He thought of the trees he had felled for no reason. He thought of the streams he had dammed to catch fish, leaving smaller pools to dry and kill the frogs.

He held out his hands. The water pooled in his palms, clear and bright. It did not turn to mud.

He ran through the forest that night as though wings were tied to his ankles. He reached his village before dawn and pressed the water to his mother's lips. Color returned to her cheeks by morning. By noon she was sitting up, asking for palm wine.

But Kembe never hunted in the deep forest again. He became a keeper of the waterways instead, tending the streams and pools with the same devotion he had once given to the chase. And sometimes, on moonlit nights, the elders said, you could still see a pale light moving between the trees where no hunter dared to follow.
moral: The forest gives its gifts only to those who take only what they need.
source: Central African oral tradition, BaAka/Mbaka folklore

title: Ah Puch and the Moon Child
summary: A young Maya girl ventures too close to the entrance of Xibalba and encounters Ah Puch, lord of death, who tests her courage and teaches her the boundary between the living and the dead.
full_text:
In the time before the Spanish ships appeared on the horizon, when the great cities of the Maya still stood whole and proud, there lived a girl named Ixchel Balam in a village near the base of the Caracol mountains. She was curious in the way that troubles elders, always asking why the smoke rose straight on certain mornings and curled on others, always pressing her ear to stones as though she expected them to speak.

Her grandmother, a woman of great knowledge, warned her about the cave at the foot of the mountain. 'That is a mouth of Xibalba,' she said. 'The underworld breathes through it. If you go there at night, when the moon is thin and the owls call in pairs, you may hear the lords of death walking. And if Ah Puch himself finds you at his threshold, you will have to answer for your curiosity.'

Ixchel listened, and she understood, but the cave called to her in a way she could not explain. One night, when the moon was a sliver of bone in the sky, she crept from her hut and walked to the cave mouth. She carried a candle made of beeswax and a small offering of cacao beans.

The air at the entrance was cold and smelled of wet limestone. She placed the cacao at the lip of the cave and held her candle forward. The flame guttered in a breath of wind that seemed to come from far below.

Then she saw him. Ah Puch stood at the edge of the candlelight, his body a ruin of decay and authority. His flesh clung to his bones in patches, and his eyes were deep sockets lit by a pale fire. He wore the ornaments of a lord, jade and shell, and his presence filled the cave with a silence so complete it had weight.

'Child,' he said, and his voice was the sound of stone settling. 'You have come to the door of my kingdom. Do you know what lies beyond?'

Ixchel trembled, but she did not run. 'I know,' she whispered. 'You are Ah Puch, and this is Xibalba, and beyond is the place where the dead walk.'

'And why have you come?'

'Because my grandmother told me not to.'

The lord of death regarded her for a long moment. Then, impossibly, he laughed. It was not a kind sound, but it was not entirely without warmth either.

'Curiosity is the oldest door,' he said. 'It opens onto every kingdom, including mine. You have brought an offering and you have not fled. These are the two things I respect.'

He reached down and picked up the cacao beans. 'I will return these to you, for you will need them. But hear me: the boundary between your world and mine is not a line in the dirt. It is a promise. The living do not enter my kingdom until their time, and the dead do not return to yours without cause. If you cross this threshold with disrespect, I will not laugh a second time.'

Ixchel nodded, and Ah Puch dissolved into the darkness like smoke into water. She walked home in the moonlight, and she never returned to the cave. But she told the story to her children, and they told it to theirs, and in that way the lesson crossed the centuries. The dead are not to be feared, her people say. They are to be honored, from a distance, with cacao and memory and the understanding that every soul has its place.
moral: The boundary between the living and the dead exists for a reason. Approach it with respect and offerings, never with arrogance, and it will teach you something about the weight of being alive.

title: The Ghoula of the Date Palm Grove
summary: A young pearl diver encounters a shape-shifting Al Ghoula in the date palm groves near Riffa, and must outwit her to survive the night.
full_text:
In the days when pearl diving was still the lifeblood of Bahrain, a young man named Jassim worked the oyster beds off the coast of Muharraq. Each morning before dawn he would wade into the shallow waters, feeling for shells with his toes, and each evening he would walk home through the date palm groves that lined the path between the sea and his village.

One sweltering night, Jassim lingered too long at the souq, bargaining over his day's harvest. By the time he turned toward home, the moon had risen high and thin, and the palm grove stretched before him like a corridor of swaying shadows. He had always hurried through these trees without thinking, but tonight something made him slow his pace. The air tasted of copper and jasmine, and somewhere in the darkness a woman was singing a lullaby he recognized from childhood.

He called out, 'Who is there?' and a figure stepped from between the trunks. She was tall and draped in black, her face hidden beneath a veil that seemed to move even when the wind did not. When she lowered the veil, Jassim saw the face of a woman so beautiful it made his chest ache. She smiled and said, 'You are late, little brother. Your mother sent me to guide you home.'

Jassim felt a warmth spread through his limbs, and his feet began to move of their own accord toward her. But a pearl diver learns to read the currents beneath still water, and something in the way the woman stood, too perfectly balanced on the soft earth, made his instincts scream. He looked down and saw that she cast no shadow beneath the moonlight.

He remembered his grandmother's warning: the Al Ghoula can wear any face, but she cannot mimic the weight of a living soul. If she lifts your burden from your shoulders, you will follow her to the salt flats and never return. Jassim gripped the diving stone that hung from his belt, its rough surface grounding him, and said, 'My mother is in Medina. You are not her messenger.'

The woman's smile widened until it split her face in a way no human jaw could allow. Her eyes went dark as deep water, and she reached for him with fingers that had too many joints. Jassim ran. He crashed through the palms with branches clawing at his face, and behind him he heard a sound like a woman laughing and a hyena screaming at the same time.

He burst from the grove into the open moonlight of the village and did not stop until he stood gasping before his mother's door. She took one look at his face and brought him inside, pressing a cup of bitter Arabic coffee into his shaking hands. 'The Ghoula walks the groves on moonless nights,' she said, though the moon had been full. 'She borrows the light to find her way.'

Jassim never walked through the palm grove alone again, and he taught his own children to carry a rough stone when they traveled after dark, for the Al Ghoula cannot hold what has already been gripped by honest hands.
moral: Cleverness and awareness of one's surroundings can protect against supernatural deception, and the wisdom of elders should never be forgotten.
source: Bahraini oral tradition, Gulf Arab folklore

title: The Ancestor Who Guarded the Forest
summary: Ema, the ancestor-spirit, protects the mountain forests of Timor and punishes those who take more than they need from the land.
full_text:
In the cool highlands above Ainaro, where the cloud forest clings to the mountain slopes and orchids grow on every branch, the people speak of Ema. Ema is not a god. Ema is not a demon. Ema is an ancestor, the first of the line, whose spirit never left the forest but instead became part of it, root and branch and mist.

Ema guards the trees. Not all trees, but the old ones, the ones that were standing when the first people climbed the mountain and looked out over the sea. These trees have names known only to Ema, and their roots hold the memory of the village in ways that no written record ever could.

One dry season, a young man named Joaquim decided to cut down one of the old trees. He wanted timber for a new house, and the old trees were straighter and stronger than the young ones that grew in the clearings. He took his axe and walked up the mountain path, humming to himself, unafraid.

He found the tree he wanted and raised his axe. But the axe would not fall. It hung in the air as if held by an invisible hand. Joaquim pulled and strained, but the axe was fixed. Then the forest went silent. Every bird stopped singing. Every insect went still. And in that silence, Ema spoke.

'You would take this tree. But this tree holds the rain. Cut it, and the water will forget how to fall on your fields. You would take its wood. But its wood holds the name of your grandmother's grandmother. Burn it, and you will forget her face. Tell me, Joaquim, is your house worth all of that?'

Joaquim was terrified. He dropped his axe and ran down the mountain. When he reached the village, he told the elders what had happened. They shook their heads and said, 'Ema does not threaten. Ema reminds. Go back tomorrow and leave an offering at the base of the tree. Then find your timber in the clearings, where the forest gives freely.'

Joaquim did as they said. He left a betel nut and a handful of rice at the tree's base, and when he returned the next day, the offering was gone. In the clearing at the forest's edge, he found three fallen trunks, dry and perfect for building. He built his house with those trunks, and he never touched the old trees again.

The people of Ainaro say that Ema still walks the cloud forest, touching the bark of the old trees with hands that are made of mist and memory. To enter the forest with respect is to walk in the presence of an ancestor. To enter it with greed is to find that the forest, like memory, can close around you and make you forget where you are.
moral: The forest remembers what humans forget. Those who take more than they need will find that the land itself resists them.

title: Abuk, the Mother of Seed
summary: In the beginning, the goddess Abuk held all the seeds of the earth within her body, and the sky god demanded she surrender them to humanity. Her defiance and eventual sacrifice shaped the eternal bond between women and the soil.
full_text:
In the time before time had a name, when the earth was still wet with the breath of creation, there lived a goddess called Abuk. She was the first woman, shaped from the red clay of the riverbank by the hands of the sky god, and within her dwelt every seed that would ever sprout from the soil — millet, sorghum, sesame, and all the plants that would feed the generations to come.

The sky god, whose name was too vast for mortal tongues, looked down upon the world and saw that humanity was hungry. He called to Abuk and commanded her to release the seeds so that the people might plant them and eat. But Abuk, wise and stubborn as the baobab that outlives a hundred droughts, shook her head. 'If I give them all the seeds at once,' she said, 'the people will become lazy and wasteful. They will feast for a season and starve in the next. Let them come to me slowly, one seed at a time, and learn the patience of the soil.'

The sky god grew angry, for his voice was the thunder and his patience was the lightning. He reached down from the heavens with a great hand and tore the seeds from Abuk's body, scattering them across the fields and forests and waterways. Where the seeds fell, crops sprang up wild and untamed, and the people gathered them with grateful hands.

But Abuk did not weep. She knelt upon the earth and pressed her palms into the mud, and from her touch came the knowledge of cultivation — the understanding of when to plant and when to harvest, when to irrigate and when to let the land rest. She whispered this knowledge to the women of the villages, and they became the keepers of the fields, the guardians of the growing things.

To this day, the women of the Dinka and Nuer peoples tend the granaries and decide when the seed is planted. They say that Abuk's spirit lives in every mortar where grain is ground, in every hand that scoops the rich earth, and in every mother who feeds her children from the harvest. The men hunt and tend cattle, but the earth's bounty belongs to Abuk and her daughters.

When the rains come late and the fields grow dry, the elders gather the women at the foot of the great anthill — Abuk's mound, they call it — and they pour a little milk upon the ground and speak her name. For they know that the goddess who once held the world's hunger in her hands will not abandon those who remember her sacrifice.
moral: Knowledge shared with patience outlasts abundance given without wisdom.
source: South Sudanese oral tradition, Nilotic folklore

title: The Al and the Shepherd's Fire
summary: A band of shepherds on the high pastures of Ararat discover that the darkness between their campfires is not empty, and that the Al watches from the space between flames.
full_text:
In the time before the Flood, when the sons of Aram tended their flocks upon Ararat, there lived a shepherd named Torgom who feared nothing. He had wrestled wolves with his bare hands and once drove a leopard from his fold with a burning brand.

But the old women whispered of the Al, and Torgom laughed at them. 'What is an Al?' he asked. 'A shadow that mothers invent to keep children from wandering.' The old women crossed themselves and said nothing.

One autumn evening, when frost silvered the high meadows, Torgom drove his flock to a hollow beneath a basalt outcropping. He built three fires in a ring and settled in to watch the night. The other shepherds slept, but Torgom kept the first vigil.

In the second hour past midnight he noticed the cold. Not the mountain's natural cold, but a cold that crept between the fires like water through cracked earth. The flames did not dim, yet the warmth fled. Torgom peered into the space between the fires.

There, where the light should have met, was a patch of darkness that did not belong. It was not merely the absence of light but a darkness with weight and substance. And within it, two eyes opened.

They burned with a cold, wet light, like marsh-fire in still water, regarding him with ancient intelligence and utter mercylessness. The Al had come.

Torgom reached for his knife, but his hand would not obey him. The Al drifted closer, tall and thin, wrapped in hair like riverweed, its mouth a wound smiling. 'You laugh at the old women,' it whispered, its voice the sound of embers collapsing. 'But they know what you do not. I am the space between every flame. Every fire you build only makes more darkness for me.'

Torgom spoke from desperation, and desperation has its own wisdom. 'Then I will sit in the dark and face you without light.' The Al laughed. 'Fool. If you build no fire, I will come as the cold.'

Yet in the forest beyond, Torgom found something the Al had not predicted. The trees groaned in a wind he could not feel, and in their groaning was a sound that predated fire, predated light, predated even the darkness the Al called home. It was the voice of the earth itself, humming where neither fire nor shadow could reach.

At dawn Torgom told the shepherds to descend to the valley, to the rivers, to places where water spoke louder than shadow. Before leaving, he poured river water over the basalt and prayed to the spirits of the deep earth to hold the Al beneath the rock.

From that day the Armenians honored both fire and water, learning that the Al cannot be defeated by flame, for it feeds upon the shadows flame creates. But it is held at bay by running water, which speaks in a voice older than darkness, and by the deep roots of trees that remember the world before the Al first opened its eyes.
moral: Disbelief does not protect against what is real; only wisdom and respect for the old ways can hold darkness at bay.

title: Al-Khidr and the Sultan of Petra
summary: When a greedy sultan attempts to claim the treasures of Petra for himself, Al-Khidr appears as a humble guide to teach him that the city of stone holds no wealth for those who do not understand its meaning.
full_text:
In the centuries after the Nabataean kingdom fell, when Petra stood empty and its carved facades crumbled under the patience of wind and rain, there came to the region a sultan from a distant land. He had heard tales of the city carved from rose-red rock, of the treasury said to hold the riches of kings, and he marched upon the site with five hundred soldiers and thirty camels loaded with rope, picks, and wooden scaffolding.

The local Bedouin watched from the ridgelines and said nothing. The elders told the sultan that Petra belonged to the stones and the spirits who dwelt within them, but the sultan laughed. He set his men to work, chipping away at the walls of the Khazneh, searching for hidden chambers of gold.

For three days they found nothing but dust and the occasional bat skeleton. The sultan grew furious and ordered his men to dig deeper. On the third night, as the camp fires burned low, a figure appeared walking through the narrow canyon of the Siq as though he had been born there.

He wore simple robes and carried nothing but a walking staff. The guards let him pass, for there was something in his bearing that made the drawn bow feel foolish. He walked directly to the sultan's tent and stood at its entrance without speaking.

'Who are you?' the sultan demanded.

'A traveller,' the stranger said. 'As you are. Though you travel with more noise.'

The sultan demanded to know if the man was a spy or a thief. Al-Khidr smiled and said he was neither, but he could show the sultan a treasure greater than anything hidden in these rocks, if the sultan was willing to leave his tools behind and walk.

They walked together through the Siq in the grey light before dawn. Al-Khidr pointed to the way the canyon walls narrowed and widened, how the Nabataeans had channelled every drop of rainwater through channels carved into the rock face. He showed the sultan the remains of a cistern so vast it could have held enough water to sustain the city for two years through drought.

'You see stones,' Al-Khidr said. 'But the Nabataeans built a civilisation on water. They carved these facades not for gold, but to prove that a people could make the desert bloom. Every channel and hidden pipe in these walls is worth more than all the gold in your homeland, because it kept ten thousand people alive where no people should have survived.'

The sultan stood in silence. He looked at the carved tombs and for the first time saw not decoration but engineering. He ordered his men to pack their tools and leave. They thought he had gone mad, but he told them they had come to rob a library and had mistaken it for a vault.

Al-Khidr watched them go from the top of the High Place of Sacrifice, where the morning light turned his robes the colour of new leaves.
moral: The greatest treasures are not gold but knowledge. Those who see only what they want to find will never understand what stands before them.

title: Asema, the Vampire of the Rainforest
summary: A vampire-like spirit from Surinamese folklore who sheds her skin at night and flies through the forest in search of blood.
full_text:
Deep in the rainforests of Suriname, where the canopy blocks out the stars and the howler monkeys scream at dawn, there is a creature that the Maroons fear above all others. The Asema is a woman by day, indistinguishable from any other. But by night, she sheds her skin like a snake, hanging it in her closet, and flies through the treetops as a ball of fire, searching for victims.

The Asema does not kill quickly. She returns night after night, drinking a little blood each time, leaving her victim weak and pale. The victim wastes away, unable to eat, unable to sleep, dreaming always of a red light approaching through the darkness. By the time the Asema has finished, there is nothing left but a shell, a body that breathes but no longer lives.

The only way to identify an Asema is to find her hidden skin. If you discover a woman's skin hanging in an unexpected place, you must sprinkle salt on it. When the Asema returns and finds her skin salted, she cannot re-enter it. She will be trapped in her spirit form, forced to wander the forest as a bodiless flame until dawn destroys her. It is a cruel fate, but the Maroons say it is the only way to stop her.

A man named Kwasi from the interior once suspected his wife of being an Asema. He followed her one night and saw her climb to the roof, where she removed her skin and flew away. Kwasi took the skin and rubbed it with pepper. When his wife returned, she could not re-enter her body. She cried and pleaded, but Kwasi was firm. At dawn, she dissolved into mist. Kwasi lived alone for the rest of his life, haunted by what he had done.

The Asema is a warning against trusting appearances. The kindest neighbor, the most loving wife, might be hiding a monstrous nature beneath her skin.
moral: The most dangerous monsters often wear familiar faces.
